name: Binary Analysis & Reverse Engineering
description: Disassembly, decompilation, binary similarity, and reverse engineering of compiled code.

uss.narrative:
The earliest listed work in this area focused on wrestling control over real-world compiled systems where source code is unavailable or unwieldy. "Inception: System-Wide Security Testing of Real-World Embedded Systems Software" (USENIX 2018) tackled the messy reality of testing firmware-grade binaries, while "Precise and Accurate Patch Presence Test for Binaries" (USENIX 2018) showed you can tell whether a security patch made it into a shipped binary without source. Alongside these, "DATA - Differential Address Trace Analysis" (USENIX 2018) pushed binary analysis toward a precise security goal, hunting address-based side channels directly in compiled crypto code. The common thread: classic program-analysis problems re-framed for the stripped, optimized binaries that defenders and attackers actually face.

The next shift was twofold. First, researchers sharpened the core binary-analysis primitives and turned them against adversarial code: "DEEPVSA" (USENIX 2019) brought deep learning to value-set analysis for postmortem forensics, and a defensive sub-thread emerged with "Fuzzification: Anti-Fuzzing Techniques" and "AntiFuzz: Impeding Fuzzing Audits of Binary Executables" (both USENIX 2019), which deliberately make binaries harder to reverse and fuzz. Second, the field broadened its targets. "Everything Old is New Again: Binary Security of WebAssembly" (USENIX 2020) extended reverse-engineering concerns to a new compilation target, and a 2021 wave matured binary-only tooling: "Breaking Through Binaries" delivered compiler-quality instrumentation for binary fuzzing, "SelectiveTaint" made static-rewriting taint tracking efficient, and "DeepReflect" reconstructed malicious functionality from binaries. Obfuscation became a first-class battleground, with "MBA-Blast" (USENIX 2021) simplifying Mixed Boolean-Arithmetic obfuscation and "Loki" (USENIX 2022) hardening obfuscation against the automated attacks that work like MBA-Blast had enabled.

By 2022 the area pivoted hard toward learning-based binary understanding and, notably, toward studying the human reverse engineer. "How Machine Learning Is Solving the Binary Function Similarity Problem" (USENIX 2022) became a reference point for binary similarity, complemented by neural disassembly in "DeepDi" (USENIX 2022) and even neural-network decompilation in "DnD: A Cross-Architecture Deep Neural Network Decompiler" (USENIX 2022). At the same time, "RE-Mind" and "Decomperson" (both USENIX 2022) opened a human-factors line, asking how analysts actually decompile and reason, rather than only building tools.

Today the area sits at two frontiers. Embedded and firmware rehosting matured into practical pipelines, with "Greenhouse" and "FirmSolo" (both USENIX 2023) enabling dynamic analysis of IoT firmware and kernel modules, and "BASECOMP" (USENIX 2023) carrying these techniques into cellular baseband. Meanwhile, the quality of the abstractions we recover became the central question: "Code is not Natural Language" (USENIX 2024) pushed semantics-oriented graph representations for binary similarity, while "Ahoy SAILR!" and "A Taxonomy of C Decompiler Fidelity Issues" (both USENIX 2024) turned a critical eye on decompiler output itself, arguing for compiler-aware structuring and systematically cataloguing where decompiled C still falls short.

ndss.narrative:
The earliest work in this area, all at NDSS 2018, tackled the classic hard problems of turning raw bytes back into analyzable code. "Superset Disassembly: Statically Rewriting x86 Binaries Without Heuristics" (NDSS 2018) attacked the ambiguity of where instructions begin by rewriting binaries without relying on brittle heuristics, while "Things You May Not Know About Android (Un)Packers" (NDSS 2018) confronted the way packing hides malware from static analysis, and "When Coding Style Survives Compilation" (NDSS 2018) showed that authorship fingerprints persist even after compilation. Together these framed the field's core tension: compiled binaries strip away structure, and recovering it is both a security tool and a security threat.

The next shift, around 2019-2021, was the arrival of machine learning as the dominant lens. Binary code similarity moved from hand-built features to learned representations, first with "Neural Machine Translation Inspired Binary Code Similarity Comparison beyond Function Pairs" (NDSS 2019) and then decisively with "DeepBinDiff: Learning Program-Wide Code Representations for Binary Diffing" (NDSS 2020). ML even reached the oldest problem of all, disassembly itself, in "XDA: Accurate, Robust Disassembly with Transfer Learning" (NDSS 2021). In parallel, a strong reverse-engineering-for-systems thread grew up alongside the code-analysis work: reconstructing CAN bus commands in "Automated Cross-Platform Reverse Engineering of CAN Bus Commands From Mobile Apps" (NDSS 2020), protocol formats in "NetPlier: Probabilistic Network Protocol Reverse Engineering from Message Traces" (NDSS 2021) and later "BinaryInferno" (NDSS 2023), and cellular basebands in "BaseSpec" (NDSS 2021) and "FirmWire" (NDSS 2022).

By 2023-2024 the two threads matured toward practical, semantics-aware tools. Binary similarity became cross-architecture vulnerability hunting in "VulHawk" (NDSS 2023), and diffing grew semantics-aware in "SigmaDiff" (NDSS 2024). The pivotal turn was decompilation meeting large language models: "DeGPT: Optimizing Decompiler Output with LLM" (NDSS 2024) used an LLM to make decompiler output readable, and this quickly generalized to recovering the names that stripping destroys, in "Unleashing the Power of Generative Model in Recovering Variable Names from Stripped Binary" (NDSS 2025) and "Beyond Classification: Inferring Function Names in Stripped Binaries via Domain Adapted LLMs" (NDSS 2025).

The most recent work, at NDSS 2026, shows the LLM wave both deepening and being scrutinized. Neural decompilation is being made more rigorous and deployable in "Idioms: A Simple and Effective Framework for Turbo-Charging Local Neural Decompilation with Well-Defined Types" (NDSS 2026), while "FidelityGPT" (NDSS 2026) uses retrieval-augmented generation to correct decompilation distortions and "Decompiling the Synergy: An Empirical Study of Human-LLM Teaming in Software Reverse Engineering" (NDSS 2026) steps back to measure how well analysts and models actually work together. At the same time the field is auditing its own ML foundations, as in "A Deep Dive into Function Inlining and its Security Implications for ML-based Binary Analysis" (NDSS 2026), and continuing the durable systems thread with firmware and PLC reverse engineering in "Through the Authentication Maze" and "Discovering Blind-Trust Vulnerabilities in PLC Binaries via State Machine Recovery" (both NDSS 2026). The area now stands at a point where generative models are reshaping decompilation and readability, even as researchers work to make those tools reliable, type-correct, and honestly evaluated.

sp.narrative:
The earliest work in this slice treats binary analysis as a representation and recovery problem. Asm2Vec (S&P 2019) learned vector embeddings of assembly so that clone search could survive compiler optimization and obfuscation, replacing brittle hand-tuned signatures with learned features. Alongside it, reverse engineering appeared as a means to an end in applied security: Self-Encrypting Deception (S&P 2019) pried open SSD firmware to expose broken full-disk encryption, showing that RE was the tool that turned closed hardware into an auditable target.

The 2020-2021 period pushed on the machinery that makes downstream analysis possible: rewriting, disassembly, and recovery. RetroWrite (S&P 2020) and StochFuzz (S&P 2021) made it practical to statically instrument and fuzz stripped, closed-source binaries, while Binsec/Rel (S&P 2020) brought relational symbolic execution to bear on constant-time verification at the binary level. Underneath all of this sat the disassembly question itself, which the community stepped back to survey in SoK: All You Ever Wanted to Know About x86/x64 Binary Disassembly (S&P 2021). Recovering the abstractions that compilers strip away became a theme in its own right, from OSPREY's probabilistic recovery of variables and data structures (S&P 2021) to the study of how compiler optimization frustrates function-signature recovery (S&P 2021).

Two shifts define the 2022-2024 middle. First, the field turned reflective and machine-learned: SoK: Demystifying Binary Lifters (S&P 2022) audited the IR-lifting layer that so many tools depend on, while XFL (S&P 2023), Callee (S&P 2023), and "Len or index or count" (S&P 2024) recast function naming, call-graph recovery, and variable naming as learning problems, using multi-label and transfer learning to hand human reverse engineers back the identifiers that stripping removed. Second, analysis broadened past x86 and past C: D-ARM (S&P 2023) tackled ARM disassembly through superset interpretation and graph modeling, QueryX (S&P 2023) let analysts run symbolic queries over decompiled code to find bugs, and Pyfet (S&P 2023) opened up Python binary decompilation for forensics.

The most recent work sharpens both the type-recovery and the language-coverage frontiers. TypeForge (S&P 2025) synthesizes and selects best-fit composite data types for stripped binaries, and CiRCLE (S&P 2026) pushes that further to reconstruct complex, fragmented data structures that defeat ordinary decompilers. Disassembly itself keeps evolving into a principled learned formulation with Disassembly as Weighted Interval Scheduling with Learned Weights (S&P 2025), while non-standard ARM binaries get dedicated data-code separation in You Can't Judge a Binary by Its Header (S&P 2025). Language coverage is now a first-class concern: PyLingual (S&P 2025) chases near-perfect decompilation of evolving Python, and Oxidizer (S&P 2026) targets concise, high-fidelity decompilation of Rust, signaling that the field is racing to keep decompilers current with the memory-safe and interpreted languages that modern software and malware actually ship in.

ccs.narrative:
Binary analysis at CCS has shifted from rule-based approaches to ML-powered symbol recovery, embedding models, and LLM-assisted decompilation. The 2018 class set the direction: Debin: Predicting Debug Information in Stripped Binaries (CCS 2018) applied conditional random fields to recover variable names and types, while VMHunt: A Verifiable Approach to Partially-Virtualized Binary Code Simplification (CCS 2018) tackled obfuscated code protected by virtual machines. Block Oriented Programming (CCS 2018) studied binary exploitation from the attacker perspective.

Large-scale unpacking infrastructure arrived with Towards Paving the Way for Large-Scale Windows Malware Analysis: Generic Binary Unpacking with Orders-of-Magnitude Performance Boost (CCS 2018), enabling malware corpus analysis at scale. FirmXRay: Detecting Bluetooth Link Layer Vulnerabilities From Bare-Metal Firmware (CCS 2020) applied static binary analysis to bare-metal IoT firmware to find BLE protocol vulnerabilities without OS support.

The 2021-2024 arc was dominated by language model approaches. PalmTree: Learning an Assembly Language Model for Instruction Embedding (CCS 2021) pre-trained a BERT-style model on assembly corpora. SymLM: Predicting Function Names in Stripped Binaries (CCS 2022) extended this to function-name recovery using execution-aware embeddings. ReSym: Harnessing LLMs to Recover Variable and Data Structure Symbols from Stripped Binaries (CCS 2024) brought GPT-class LLMs to full struct and variable symbol recovery in decompiled output.

top4.narrative:
The earliest work in this list treated binary analysis as a problem of recovering the information that compilation and stripping throw away. Debin: Predicting Debug Information in Stripped Binaries (CCS 2018) used learned models to guess debug symbols back into stripped code, while Superset Disassembly (NDSS 2018) tackled the still-unsolved foundation of the field — reliably deciding where instructions begin — well enough to rewrite x86 binaries without heuristics. Alongside these, a cluster of papers pushed on practical targets that resist source-level tooling: unpacking malware at scale (Towards Paving the Way for Large-Scale Windows Malware Analysis, CCS 2018), simplifying virtualized code (VMHunt, CCS 2018), finding address-based side channels (DATA, USENIX 2018), and testing embedded firmware (Inception, USENIX 2018). The common thread was that once you only have the compiled artifact, even basic questions become hard.

The decisive shift was learning representations of code rather than hand-writing analyses. Asm2Vec (S&P 2019) showed that assembly could be embedded into vectors robust to obfuscation and compiler optimization, turning binary clone search into a similarity problem; DeepBinDiff (NDSS 2020) extended this to program-wide diffing, and PalmTree (CCS 2021) built a general pre-trained assembly language model that many downstream tasks could reuse. This wave carried into recovering higher-level structure — OSPREY (S&P 2021) inferred variables and data structures from stripped binaries probabilistically, and SymLM (CCS 2022) predicted function names — and into cross-architecture vulnerability search (VulHawk, NDSS 2023). Amid the enthusiasm, How Machine Learning Is Solving the Binary Function Similarity Problem (USENIX 2022) served as a sobering, careful benchmark of what actually works. At the same time the field kept maturing its foundations and its instrumentation tooling: SoK: All You Ever Wanted to Know About x86/x64 Binary Disassembly (S&P 2021) systematized how hard disassembly really is, while RetroWrite (S&P 2020) and Breaking Through Binaries (USENIX 2021) made static rewriting good enough for fuzzing and sanitization of closed-source binaries.

The most recent turn is toward large language models and toward the messy, high-value target of decompilation. DeGPT (NDSS 2024) used an LLM to clean up decompiler output, ReSym (CCS 2024) harnessed LLMs to recover variable and data-structure symbols, and USENIX 2024's Code is not Natural Language argued for semantics-oriented graph representations over treating assembly like text. The 2026 NDSS crop shows the area consolidating around these threads: Idioms turbo-charges local neural decompilation with well-defined types, FidelityGPT corrects decompilation distortions via retrieval-augmented generation, and Decompiling the Synergy studies how humans and LLMs actually team up during reverse engineering. Others revisit long-standing concerns with fresh eyes — A Deep Dive into Function Inlining probes how a basic compiler transform quietly breaks ML-based binary analysis, while vSim and Enhancing Semantic-Aware Binary Diffing push similarity and diffing toward value- and semantics-aware precision. The field has moved from recovering symbols by hand to learned embeddings, and now to LLM-assisted decompilation whose reliability is itself becoming the research question.
